paras: The attempted lynching of Victor Sebree took place at Rio Grande City, Starr County, Texas, in September 1888, when armed Mexican residents tried to seize Sebree, a United States customs officer, after he shot the editor Catarino E. Garza in a street fight. Sebree escaped to Fort Ringgold, whose commander refused to give him up, while the crowd held the town and cut its telegraph line. No one was killed, and papers across the country reported the episode as a border uprising threatening a "massacre" of American citizens.

According to a letter from Rio Grande City published by the Austin Weekly Statesman, the trouble began on May 16, 1888, when Sebree, assisting Sheriff W. W. Sheely, killed Abraham Recendez, a robbery suspect who resisted his guards. The letter said a political club led by Augustine and Silverio de la Pena, opposed to Sheely, engaged Garza, who published a Spanish-language paper at Corpus Christi, to speak and write against the Americans, and that his paper called Sebree "an assassin, a coward." Wire reports added that Sebree had brought a criminal libel suit against Garza.

The letter placed the fight on the evening of September 21, while other reports dated it Saturday, September 22. In the letter's account, Sebree asked Garza whether he wanted to fight, Garza's companion Lopez opened fire first, and Sebree shot Garza in the abdomen and Lopez in the leg without being hit. Sebree then rode for Ringgold barracks, pursued by mounted Mexicans who fired at him, and Colonel Clendenin put him in the guardhouse.

A mob of about one hundred armed men announced its intention of lynching Sebree and went to his room, the letter said, and about 200 later entered the reservation to demand him. The commander refused and, according to the Associated Press, warned that any attempt to take him would draw the fire of the Gatling guns. Through the night the crowd paraded the streets, besieged the telegraph office and cut the government line.

Sheriff Sheely telegraphed the governor that more than 100 armed men wanted Sebree jailed, where "he will be lynched," and that his own life was threatened if he refused. Governor L. S. Ross told him not to jail Sebree until he could be protected from mob violence and ordered rangers and nearby sheriffs with posses to the town. By September 24 the town was reported quiet pending a conference between a committee from the mob and the sheriff, though the New York Tribune's correspondent wrote on September 26 that the mob still held it.

On September 28 Sebree was brought before County Judge Kelsey, waived examination and, in default of bail, was committed to the Brownsville jail because the local jail was not thought safe. Most prints gave the bond as $2,500 and one as $500. A cavalry troop was sent to reinforce the fort, while prominent residents asked the government for a commission of inquiry instead. In early October Garza and Jose Lopez were reported arrested at Rio Grande, and no arrest of anyone in the mob appears in the coverage found.

The story first ran on September 24 as a Brownsville dispatch headed "Terrorized by a Mob," which described "Four Hundred Mexican Bandits" demanding "the Blood of a Government Inspector." Associated Press copy and a New York Herald special from Austin then appeared from Washington and Richmond to Sacramento, Kansas, Wisconsin and Nebraska. The wire called the crowd "the lowest class of bandits and smugglers," and the Austin Weekly Statesman headed its report "Dusky Sons of the Montezumas On the Rampage."

The Herald special warned of a "general massacre" of Texas citizens, noted that Mexicans outnumbered "the white citizens" ten to one, and yet observed that its telegrams, all from the county judge or sheriff, were each "more startling and sensational than the other." Accounts of the fight came almost entirely from Sebree's side, and no statement from Garza, Lopez or the crowd appears in the coverage. Weekly digests still reported in October that Sebree had "shot and killed" Garza.

The Herald special and later digests said Garza was killed, the first wire and the letter called him mortally wounded, and dispatches from Rio Grande City said he would probably recover. The reports from the town itself, the closer evidence, described him as critical on September 28 and arrested in October. Estimates of the crowd ranged from about 100 to 400, and only the letter said that Lopez fired first.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Victor Sebree
bases: Armed crowds pursued and fired on Sebree, announced their intention of lynching him and demanded him from the post commander and the sheriff, who kept him in military custody (A1, A14, A15).

A crowd of 100 to 400 armed men sought without legal authority to seize and lynch Sebree in vengeance for his shooting of Garza, but he was protected at Fort Ringgold and no one was killed (A14, A15, A8).

The Brownsville wire, the AP dispatch from Rio Grande City, the collector's telegrams, the sheriff's telegrams and a letter from Rio Grande City independently describe the shooting, the pursuit and the mob's demand for Sebree, though all come from the American and official side (A1, A8, A6, A15, A14).

accounts.label: Sheriff's telegram

accounts.label: Associated Press, Rio Grande City
accounts.gist: Garza, shot Friday, was alive; Sebree, pursued and fired on, surrendered to the commander, who refused the Mexicans' demand and threatened Gatling-gun fire.

accounts.label: Brownsville wire
accounts.gist: A mob of 400 bandits and smugglers held the town; Garza mortally wounded; 200 demanded Sebree at the fort.

accounts.label: New York Herald special from Austin
accounts.gist: Sebree killed Garza; over 150 armed Mexicans tried to lynch him; massacre feared; the alarming telegrams came from the county judge and sheriff.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'Terrorized by a Mob' and 'Four Hundred Mexican Bandits ... Demanding the Blood of a Government Inspector' cast the crowd as bandits and Sebree as an officer under siege.
The Austin Weekly Statesman condemned the 'furious mob' under the headline 'Dusky Sons of the Montezumas On the Rampage' and called the rioters 'the lowest class of Mexicans'.
The Herald special warned of a 'general massacre' of Texas citizens but noted the alarming telegrams all came from the county judge or sheriff and grew more 'sensational'.
The New York Tribune's special gave the officials' background and said other dispatches 'have not given the facts'.

The letter written on September 22 says 'yesterday evening'; the sheriff's telegram dated September 23 says 'yesterday'.

info: Street fight on the evening of Friday, September 21, 1888 (letter dated Sept 22 says 'yesterday evening'; AP says 'Friday last') or Saturday, September 22 (Evening Star, Herald, sheriff's telegram of Sept 23 'yesterday'); siege of the town September 22-26.
Main street of Rio Grande City; Sebree sheltered at Fort Ringgold (Ringgold barracks).
Victor Sebree (spelled Seebree, Sebrese, Sebre, Lebree, Zebre), a United States customs inspector or revenue officer; the target of the mob. Not killed or injured.
Sebree shot editor Catarino E. Garza in the abdomen and his companion Lopez in the leg in a street fight; the mob demanded vengeance for the shooting.

Armed Mexican residents of Rio Grande City and the surrounding country, called by the papers 'bandits and smugglers' and linked by officials to the Pena political club and the Mexican revolutionary Martinez.
Sebree protected by the garrison; waived examination, bond $2,500 (or $500), committed to Brownsville jail in Sheriff Brito's charge; town reported quiet by Sept 28.
